To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
serotonergic agonist administration to the intact or spinal fetal rat promotes fetal motor behavior.
serotonergic agonist-induced hindlimb stepping was not dependent on an intact descending pathway from the brainstem.

the serotonergic agonist quipazine increases fetal activity and promotes the occurrence of hindlimb stepping, and that quipazine also promotes hindlimb stepping and increases hindlimb activity after spinal transection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of serotonergics on the fetal rat brain and spinal cord, and the possible role of serotonin in the development of fetal motor activity.
the development of the central nervous system and its regulation by the endogenous neurotransmitter serotonin (5-HT).
the role of the developing 5-HT system in regulating fetal behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fetal rat spinal cord is not necessary for the expression of 5-HT-induced stepping.

1) serotonergic agonism induces motor activity and stepping in fetal rats; 2) the serotonergic agonist quipazine induces stepping in spinal fetal rats; 3) the serotoneric agonists quipize and alpha-Me5-HT promote stepping in intact fetal rats; and 4) serotonergic activation modulates the motor system at multiple levels of development.
serotonergic agonist administration increases fetal motor behavior and induces hindlimb stepping.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the serotonergic agonist-induced hindlimb stepping is a result of a combination of effects on both supraspinal and spinal mechanisms.
the fetal 5HT system is a modulator of motor activity at multiple sites of the developing central neural axis.
the serotonergic system in the fetus is involved in the regulation of motor behavior, and that this system is functional in the absence of the brainstem.
The main takeaway from our work is that

serotonergic agonist administration to fetal rats can induce fetal stepping and hindlimb activity, and this effect is present in spinal fetuses, indicating that spinal cord circuitry is sufficient to generate these behaviors.
